# Mosaic plots {#sec-mosaic-plots}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(patchwork)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
library(ggmosaic)
source("_common.R")
# use font
showtext::showtext_auto()
# set theme
ggplot2::theme_set(fmggp2::theme_titanic(
    base_size = 12))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Theme: `theme_titanic()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_titanic()`, modeled on Titanic (1997), using the Vallejo Titanic Colors paint set: a hull black background, a yellow hull stripe frame and title, a canvas plot area with deck planking grid lines, antifouling red, faded yellow, stone, and wood deck marks, and a Big Caslon title.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggmosaic)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1997)
titanic_fans <- tibble(
  fan_id = 1:500,
  age_group = sample(c("Teen", "Adult"), 500, replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(0.4, 0.6))) |>
  mutate(
    viewings = if_else(age_group == "Teen",
      sample(c("Once", "Twice", "3+ times"), n(), replace = TRUE,
        prob = c(0.35, 0.35, 0.30)),
      sample(c("Once", "Twice", "3+ times"), n(), replace = TRUE,
        prob = c(0.70, 0.22, 0.08))),
    soundtrack = if_else(
      runif(n()) < c(Once = 0.25, Twice = 0.50, `3+ times` = 0.80)[viewings],
      "Yes", "No"),
    age_group = factor(age_group, levels = c("Teen", "Adult")),
    viewings = factor(viewings, levels = c("Once", "Twice", "3+ times")),
    soundtrack = factor(soundtrack, levels = c("No", "Yes")))
labs_mosaic <- labs(
      title = "Titanic",
      caption = "Simulated data",
      subtitle = "500 moviegoers in 1998",
      fill = "Age group")
ggp2_mosaic <- ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
   ggmosaic::geom_mosaic(mapping =
          aes(x = product(viewings, age_group),
              fill = age_group)) +
    scale_x_productlist("Age group") +
    scale_y_productlist("Times seen in theaters") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          panel.grid.major = element_blank())
ggp2_mosaic +
    labs_mosaic
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
✅ at least two categorical variables
:::

::::

## Description

A mosaic plot shows how many rows fall where two sets of groups meet, with boxes that change in how wide and how high they are. It works like a bar graph with its parts put one on top of the other,[^stacked] but that bar graph shows how big each part is with only how high it goes and its color. A mosaic plot also uses how wide each box is.[^width]

Put the key[^legend] of a mosaic plot above or below it, and run the key from left to right. That keeps the form of the mosaic plot and makes it easier to read.

We can make mosaic plots with [`ggmosaic`.](https://haleyjeppson.github.io/ggmosaic/)[^ggmosaic]

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Bring in the code we'll use.[^packages]
:::


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_mosaic
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
# pak::pak("haleyjeppson/ggmosaic")
library(ggmosaic)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
*Titanic* was a movie from 1997 about a big ship that went down in the sea. A teen is a young person who is close to growing up, and an adult is a person who has grown up. It played in movie houses for months, and lots of fans (most of all teens) went back to see it again and again. We'll make up[^simulate] 500 people who saw the movie, in three steps where each step builds on the one before. First, `sample()` picks whether each fan is a teen or an adult (`age_group`). Next, each age group gets its own chances of seeing the movie once, two times, or three or more times (`viewings`). The soundtrack is the music from the movie, sold on its own. Last, the more times a fan saw the movie, the more likely they were to buy the soundtrack (`soundtrack`). So `runif()` picks a number between 0 and 1 and checks whether it falls below the chance for the number of times that fan saw the movie.[^runif] Starting with `set.seed()`[^seed] means you'll get the same 500 fans every time you run the code below.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_mosaic
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1997) # same 500 fans every time the code runs
titanic_fans <- tibble(
  fan_id = 1:500, # 500 different fans, one row each
  age_group = sample(
    c("Teen", "Adult"), 500, # each fan is a teen or an adult
    replace = TRUE, # groups repeat across fans
    prob = c(0.4, 0.6) # a few more adults than teens
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    viewings = if_else(age_group == "Teen",
      sample(c("Once", "Twice", "3+ times"), n(), replace = TRUE,
        prob = c(0.35, 0.35, 0.30)), # teens go back to the theater more often
      sample(c("Once", "Twice", "3+ times"), n(), replace = TRUE,
        prob = c(0.70, 0.22, 0.08)) # most adults see it once
      ),
    soundtrack = if_else(
      runif(n()) < c(Once = 0.25, Twice = 0.50, `3+ times` = 0.80)[viewings], # more viewings, more likely to buy
      "Yes", "No"),
    age_group = factor(age_group, levels = c("Teen", "Adult")),
    viewings = factor(viewings, levels = c("Once", "Twice", "3+ times")), # fewest to most viewings
    soundtrack = factor(soundtrack, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
    )
glimpse(titanic_fans)
```
:::

## Distribution

A mosaic plot turns a table of how many rows fall where two groups meet[^two-way] into a set of boxes.[^rect] How wide each box is, and how high it is, are both chances.[^prob] We built a link between age group and `viewings`[^dependence] into the code that makes up the data, so we know how wide and how high those boxes should be. Below we'll move from the fans, to a graph, to the rule behind it.[^formula]

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first eight fans.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_mosaic
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(titanic_fans, 8)
```
:::

All five teens in this group saw the movie more than once, while two of the three adults saw it only once. The table below finds how many fans fall where each age group meets each number of `viewings`, then turns each number into a share of its age group.[^proportion]

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_mosaic
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
titanic_fans |>
  count(age_group, viewings) |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 2)) |>
  ungroup()
```
:::

Teens fall in close to the same numbers across seeing the movie once, two times, and three or more times, while about two thirds of adults saw the movie once.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

The mosaic plot below shows the table above. Each age group is as wide as its share of all the fans (adults take up more room because there are more of them).[^width-share] Each box is as high as the share of its age group that saw the movie that number of times.[^height-share]

The second mosaic plot puts the values of `viewings` in a new order with `sample()`.[^shuffle] That keeps how many fans saw the movie once, two times, and three or more times, but breaks the link between age group and `viewings`. Without the link, the boxes line up straight across the graph: every age group has the same shares of once, two times, and three or more times.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_mosaic
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
  ggmosaic::geom_mosaic(aes(x = product(viewings, age_group),
                            fill = viewings)) +
  scale_x_productlist("Age group") +
  scale_y_productlist("Viewings") +
  labs(title = "Simulated", fill = "Viewings") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major = element_blank())

titanic_fans |>
  mutate(viewings = sample(viewings)) |>
  ggplot() +
  ggmosaic::geom_mosaic(aes(x = product(viewings, age_group),
                            fill = viewings)) +
  scale_x_productlist("Age group") +
  scale_y_productlist("Viewings") +
  labs(title = "Shuffled", fill = "Viewings") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major = element_blank())
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

The area of each box is [the chance that a fan falls in both groups at once](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_probability_distribution),[^joint] which we can break into how wide the box is times how high it is:

$$
P(\text{age}, \text{viewings}) = \underbrace{P(\text{age})}_{\text{width}} \times \underbrace{P(\text{viewings} \mid \text{age})}_{\text{height}}
$$

The code that makes up the data sets how wide the boxes are with $P(\text{Teen}) = 0.4$ and $P(\text{Adult}) = 0.6$, and how high they are with [a different rule for each age group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability_distribution):[^conditional] $(0.35, 0.35, 0.30)$ for teens and $(0.70, 0.22, 0.08)$ for adults.

When two columns have [no link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_(probability_theory)),[^independent] $P(\text{viewings} \mid \text{age}) = P(\text{viewings})$, so the boxes for every age group are as high as each other. That's what the second mosaic plot shows. The more the boxes for one age group are out of line with the boxes for the next, the stronger the link.[^relationship] Try giving adults the same chances of seeing the movie once, two times, and three or more times as teens, and the first mosaic plot will look like the second.


## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::

  -   Make the words around the graph[^labels] with `labs()`

  -   Start the graph with `ggplot()` and give it `data`

  -   Put the `product()` of `viewings` and `age_group` on the `x` axis[^product]

  -   Join `age_group` to `fill` so each age group gets its own color[^fill]

  -   `geom_mosaic()` names the axes after the columns, so set the words on each axis[^axis-titles] with `scale_x_productlist()` and `scale_y_productlist()`

  -   Take away the lines behind the boxes[^grid] and move the key below the graph with `theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major = element_blank())`


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_mosaic
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
labs_mosaic <- labs(
      title = "Titanic",
      caption = "Simulated data",
      subtitle = "500 moviegoers in 1998",
      fill = "Age group")
ggp2_mosaic <- ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
   ggmosaic::geom_mosaic(mapping =
          aes(x = product(viewings, age_group),
              fill = age_group)) +
    scale_x_productlist("Age group") +
    scale_y_productlist("Times seen in theaters") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          panel.grid.major = element_blank())
ggp2_mosaic +
    labs_mosaic
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: run_graph_mosaic
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_mosaic <- labs(
      title = "Titanic",
      caption = "Simulated data",
      subtitle = "500 moviegoers in 1998",
      fill = "Age group")
ggp2_mosaic <- ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
   ggmosaic::geom_mosaic(mapping =
          aes(x = product(viewings, age_group),
              fill = age_group)) +
    scale_x_productlist("Age group") +
    scale_y_productlist("Times seen in theaters") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          panel.grid.major = element_blank())
ggp2_mosaic +
    labs_mosaic
```
:::

### Details

We've changed the words around the mosaic plot (`ggp2_mosaic`) to show what's going on in the `aes()` of `geom_mosaic()`.

::: {.column-margin}
::: {style="font-size: 0.95em; color: #5f2042;"}
It's a good idea to change the `fig-height` and `fig-width` of your graph
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: create_table_mosaic
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| fig-align: center
# graph
labs_mosaic <- labs(
      title = "Titanic",
      caption = "Simulated data",
      subtitle = "f(viewings | age_group) f(age_group)",
      fill = "Age group")
ggp2_mosaic <- ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
   ggmosaic::geom_mosaic(mapping =
          aes(x = product(viewings, age_group),
              fill = age_group)) +
    scale_x_productlist("Age group") +
    scale_y_productlist("Times seen in theaters") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          panel.grid.major = element_blank())
ggp2_mosaic +
    labs_mosaic
# table
titanic_counts <- titanic_fans |>
    dplyr::count(viewings, age_group) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = age_group, values_from = n) |>
    dplyr::arrange(desc(viewings))
```
:::


The table below shows how many fans fall where each age group meets each number of `viewings`. As we can see, the graph shows these numbers with how high and how wide each box is.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
kableExtra::kable_paper(
  kable_input = knitr::kable(titanic_counts),
  font_size = 14)
```


## More info

It's worth reading [the long help page for `ggmosaic`](https://haleyjeppson.github.io/ggmosaic/articles/ggmosaic.html),[^vignette] most of all the parts on putting groups in order and on looking at one column inside each group of another column.[^conditioning]

### Two variables

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: titanic_2var_counts_table
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# table
titanic_2var_counts <- titanic_fans |>
    dplyr::count(viewings, soundtrack) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(
      names_from = soundtrack,
      values_from = n) |>
    dplyr::arrange(desc(viewings))

kableExtra::kable_paper(
  kable_input = knitr::kable(titanic_2var_counts),
  font_size = 12)
```
:::


Below is another mosaic plot of two columns. It puts `viewings` and `soundtrack` in `product()`, and joins `soundtrack` to `fill`.[^map-2var]

Once again we can see how many fans fall where two groups meet in the table:[^crosstab]

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: ggp2_mosaic_2var
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| error: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
# build 2-variable mosaic plot
labs_mosaic_2var <- labs(
  title = "Titanic",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "2-Variable plot",
  fill = "soundtrack")

ggp2_mosaic_2var <- ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
  geom_mosaic(aes(
    x = product(viewings, soundtrack),
    fill = soundtrack)) +
  scale_x_productlist("Bought the soundtrack?") +
  scale_y_productlist("Times seen in theaters") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.major = element_blank())

ggp2_mosaic_2var +
    labs_mosaic_2var
```
:::


To look at `viewings` inside each group of another column,[^cond-var] we put `viewings` in `product()` and join `viewings` to `fill`, but we also give `conds` a column (as `product(soundtrack)`).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: ggp2_mosaic_cond
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
# build conditional mosaic plot
labs_mosaic_cond <- labs(
  title = "Titanic",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Conditional plot",
  fill = "viewings")
ggp2_mosaic_cond <- ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
  geom_mosaic(aes(
    x = product(viewings), # product variable
    fill = viewings,
    conds = product(soundtrack))) + # conditional variable
  scale_x_productlist("Bought the soundtrack?") +
  scale_y_productlist("Times seen in theaters") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.major = element_blank())

ggp2_mosaic_cond +
    labs_mosaic_cond
```
:::

### Facets

Another way to look at one column inside each group of another column is with small graphs.[^facets] In the example below we use `soundtrack` in both `x` and `fill` (remember to put `soundtrack` inside `product()`).

The `divider` choice[^argument] lets us pick how the boxes are cut up (up and down, or across).[^divider] Below are the two up and down choices for `divider`.[^vertical]

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
```{r}
#| label: patchwork_mosaic_run_v
#| fig-asp: 1.1
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| error: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_mosaic_facet <- labs(
        title = "Titanic",
        caption = "divider = 'vspine'",
        fill = "soundtrack")
ggp2_mosaic_vspine <- ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
          ggmosaic::geom_mosaic(aes(x = product(soundtrack),
                                 fill = soundtrack),
                              divider = "vspine") +
                    facet_grid(. ~ viewings) +
            scale_x_productlist("Times seen in theaters") +
            scale_y_productlist("Soundtrack?") +
            theme(
                axis.text.x = element_blank(),
                axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
                panel.grid.major = element_blank()) +
            labs_mosaic_facet +
            labs(caption = "divider = 'vspine'")

ggp2_mosaic_vbar <- ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
          ggmosaic::geom_mosaic(aes(x = product(soundtrack),
                                 fill = soundtrack),
                              divider = "vbar") +
                    facet_grid(. ~ viewings) +
            scale_x_productlist("Times seen in theaters") +
            scale_y_productlist("Soundtrack?") +
            theme(
                axis.text.x = element_blank(),
                axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
                panel.grid.major = element_blank()) +
            labs_mosaic_facet +
            labs(caption = "divider = 'vbar'")

ggp2_mosaic_vspine +
    ggp2_mosaic_vbar +
  patchwork::plot_layout(
    nrow = 2, guides = 'collect')
```
:::


The two across choices make the words on the axes harder to read, so we have to change these by hand.[^horizontal]

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
```{r}
#| label: patchwork_mosaic_run_h
#| fig-asp: 1.1
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| error: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
ggp2_mosaic_hspine <- ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
          ggmosaic::geom_mosaic(aes(x = product(soundtrack),
                                 fill = soundtrack),
                              divider = "hspine") +
                    facet_grid(. ~ viewings) +
            theme(
                axis.text.x = element_blank(),
                axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
                panel.grid.major = element_blank()) +
            labs_mosaic_facet +
            labs(caption = "divider = 'hspine'")


ggp2_mosaic_hbar <- ggplot(data = titanic_fans) +
          ggmosaic::geom_mosaic(aes(x = product(soundtrack),
                                 fill = soundtrack),
                              divider = "hbar") +
                    facet_grid(. ~ viewings) +
            theme(
                axis.text.x = element_blank(),
                axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
                panel.grid.major = element_blank()) +
            labs_mosaic_facet +
            labs(caption = "divider = 'hbar'")

ggp2_mosaic_hspine +
    ggp2_mosaic_hbar +
  patchwork::plot_layout(
    nrow = 2, guides = 'collect')
```
:::

[^stacked]: A stacked bar graph.

[^width]: Instead of only relying on height and color to display the relative amount for each value, mosaic plots also use width.

[^legend]: The legend. Position it on top or bottom and justify it horizontally to preserve the shape of the plot and improve readability.

[^ggmosaic]: The `ggmosaic` package, a `ggplot2` extension.

[^packages]: Install and load the packages.

[^simulate]: Simulate. The three steps are linked: each one depends on the step before it.

[^runif]: `runif()` draws a uniform random number between 0 and 1, and the fan buys the soundtrack when that number is below the probability for their number of viewings (0.25, 0.50, or 0.80).

[^seed]: Setting the random seed.

[^two-way]: A two way table (contingency table) of the counts for each combination of the two categorical variables.

[^rect]: Rectangles, also called tiles.

[^prob]: Each rectangle's width and height are probabilities.

[^dependence]: The dependence between `age_group` and `viewings`.

[^formula]: The formula.

[^proportion]: The counts for every combination of age group and viewings, converted to proportions within each age group (`share`).

[^width-share]: The width of each column of tiles is the marginal proportion of fans in that age group.

[^height-share]: The height of each tile is the conditional proportion of that age group with each number of viewings.

[^shuffle]: Shuffling (randomly permuting) `viewings` with `sample()`.

[^joint]: A joint probability, split into a width (the marginal probability) times a height (the conditional probability).

[^conditional]: A conditional distribution of `viewings` for each age group.

[^independent]: Independent variables.

[^relationship]: The stronger the relationship (dependence) between the two variables.

[^labels]: The labels (title, subtitle, caption, axis titles, and legend title).

[^product]: Map the `product()` of `viewings` and `age_group` to the `x` axis.

[^fill]: Map `age_group` to the `fill` aesthetic.

[^axis-titles]: The axis titles. `geom_mosaic()` names the axes after the variables.

[^grid]: The grid lines.

[^vignette]: The `ggmosaic` vignette.

[^conditioning]: The sections on ordering and conditioning.

[^map-2var]: Map the `product()` variables as `viewings` and `soundtrack`, and the `fill` variable as `soundtrack`.

[^crosstab]: The counts for each category in the cross tabulation.

[^cond-var]: Conditional variables. `conds` is the conditioning aesthetic in `geom_mosaic()`.

[^facets]: Facets, which include a conditioning variable.

[^argument]: The `divider` argument.

[^divider]: The spine partitions, vertical or horizontal.

[^vertical]: The two vertical orientation options, `"vspine"` and `"vbar"`.

[^horizontal]: The two horizontal orientation options (`"hspine"` and `"hbar"`) make the axis text harder to read, so it needs to be manipulated manually.
